mu1.title: SI units, prefixes and significant figures

questions.prompt: Which are the SI base units of pressure?
Convert 2.4 mm² into m².
Convert 35 cm³ into m³.
How many significant figures are in 0.00450?
scheme: 4, 5 and the final 0 are significant; the leading zeros are not.

questions.prompt: An equation has matching units on both sides. What can you conclude?
options: It is homogeneous, but could still be incorrect
scheme: A dimensionless constant or a condition of validity can still be wrong.

questions.prompt: A balance always reads 0.20 g too high. What type of error is this?
options: An error removed by averaging alone
scheme: The same offset biases every reading. Correct the zero.

questions.prompt: Times are 8.2 s, 8.4 s and 8.6 s. What is the half-range uncertainty?
Each endpoint of a distance has uncertainty ±0.5 mm. What is the absolute uncertainty in the distance?
scheme: Add the two absolute uncertainties: 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 mm.

questions.prompt: A measured time for 20 oscillations is (30.0 ± 0.2) s. What is the uncertainty in one period?
scheme: Divide the time and its absolute uncertainty by 20: 0.2/20 = 0.01 s.

questions.prompt: Repeated readings have little scatter but are far from the accepted value. They are…
options: evidence that there is no uncertainty
scheme: Small spread means precision; proximity to the true value determines accuracy.

questions.prompt: A length is (40.0 ± 0.8) cm. What is its percentage uncertainty?
A diameter has a 2% uncertainty. What is the percentage uncertainty in area A = πd²/4?
scheme: The power is 2, so double the percentage uncertainty.

questions.prompt: V has 3% uncertainty and I has 2%. What is the percentage uncertainty in R = V/I?
h has 1% uncertainty and t has 2%. What is the percentage uncertainty in g = 2h/t²?
A result is 9.8 m s⁻² with 3% uncertainty. What is its absolute uncertainty before rounding?
scheme: 0.03 × 9.8 = 0.294 m s⁻², normally reported as ±0.3 m s⁻².

mu4.title: Graphs, gradients and worst acceptable lines

questions.prompt: A graph of h / m against t² / s² has gradient 4.90. What is g?
The best gradient is 2.00 and the worst acceptable gradient is 2.12. What is the percentage uncertainty?
Which line is a valid worst acceptable line?
options: Any line joining the first and last readings
The steepest or shallowest line that crosses every error bar
A line through the origin even if it misses the bars
scheme: Every supplied error bar constrains the acceptable straight line.

questions.prompt: What are the units of the gradient of force / N against extension / m?
scheme: Vertical unit divided by horizontal unit: N/m.

questions.prompt: Which points should you normally use for a gradient triangle?
options: Two well-separated points on the best-fit line
The largest and smallest y values regardless of the line
scheme: A large triangle reduces the percentage effect of reading coordinates.

questions.prompt: When investigating resistance against wire length, which variable should be controlled?
scheme: Heating changes resistivity, so temperature should be kept as constant as practicable.

questions.prompt: Which is an appropriate table heading?
options: Length (with m written in every cell)
scheme: A heading identifies the quantity and unit; the entries contain the numerical readings.

questions.prompt: A result is (9.7 ± 0.3) m s⁻². Is the accepted value 9.81 m s⁻² within this interval?
options: Only if they have identical digits
Uncertainty cannot be used for comparisons
scheme: The accepted value lies within the estimated interval, so it is consistent with the result at this uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Which improvement directly reduces the percentage effect of stopwatch reaction time?
options: Time one oscillation instead of twenty
Time twenty complete oscillations and divide by twenty
scheme: The measured interval becomes larger while the start/stop reaction uncertainty is similar.

mu6.title: Mixed exam practice: measurements and uncertainties

questions.prompt: Which is an SI base unit?
What is 4.0 cm² in m²?
How many significant figures are in 0.0300?
Which action addresses a systematic zero error?
Three readings are 4.8 s, 5.0 s and 5.2 s. What is the half-range uncertainty?
A radius has 3% uncertainty. What is the percentage uncertainty in the volume of a sphere?
What is the uncertainty in the difference of (10.0 ± 0.1) cm and (8.0 ± 0.1) cm?
A worst acceptable straight line must…
options: use only the first and last bars

questions.prompt: For T² = (4π²/k)m, the gradient of T² against m equals…
Why measure a wire diameter at different positions and orientations?
options: To detect variation and estimate a representative diameter
To eliminate the need to measure length

questions.prompt: A student measures the diameter of a wire as (0.50 ± 0.01) mm and its length as (1.20 ± 0.01) m. Calculate the cross-sectional area of the wire in m².
scheme: C1 · A = πd²/4 with d = 0.50 × 10⁻³ m

questions.prompt: A student measures the diameter of a wire as (0.50 ± 0.01) mm and its length as (1.20 ± 0.01) m. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the cross-sectional area.
scheme: A1 · Area ∝ diameter², so percentage area uncertainty = 4%

questions.prompt: A student measures the diameter of a wire as (0.50 ± 0.01) mm and its length as (1.20 ± 0.01) m. The measured resistance is (6.0 ± 0.1) Ω. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the resistivity ρ = RA/L.
The times for 20 complete oscillations are 31.2 s, 31.6 s and 31.4 s. Calculate the mean period.
The times for 20 complete oscillations are 31.2 s, 31.6 s and 31.4 s. Use half the range to estimate the absolute uncertainty in the period.
The times for 20 complete oscillations are 31.2 s, 31.6 s and 31.4 s. Explain why averaging these times will not remove an uncorrected systematic timing error.
scheme: B1 · A systematic error biases all readings consistently, so averaging does not remove the bias

questions.prompt: A graph of height h against time squared t² has best-fit gradient 4.86 m s⁻² and worst acceptable gradient 5.02 m s⁻². The model is h = ½gt². Calculate g from the best-fit gradient.
A graph of height h against time squared t² has best-fit gradient 4.86 m s⁻² and worst acceptable gradient 5.02 m s⁻². The model is h = ½gt². Calculate the absolute uncertainty in g.
scheme: A1 · Δg = 2 × 0.16 = 0.32 m s⁻² (about 0.3 m s⁻²)

questions.prompt: A graph of height h against time squared t² has best-fit gradient 4.86 m s⁻² and worst acceptable gradient 5.02 m s⁻². The model is h = ½gt². A proposed worst-fit line crosses the first and last error bars but misses a middle bar. Explain whether it is acceptable.
scheme: B1 · It is not acceptable: a worst acceptable straight line must intersect every error bar

questions.prompt: A student wants to investigate how the period of a mass–spring oscillator depends on mass, using T = 2π√(m/k). Describe the measurements, accuracy steps and graph analysis needed to test the relationship and determine k. Include one relevant safety precaution.
levels: Level 3 (5–6)
A clear workable method over a range of masses, accurate measurement of period, correct linear graph and extraction of k, with a relevant safety precaution. Logical and sufficiently detailed.
Level 2 (3–4)
A workable method with some accuracy steps and graph analysis, but important details are missing.
Level 1 (1–2)
Some relevant apparatus, measurements or analysis, with limited detail.
indicative: Clamp a spring securely; add known masses including the hanger
Use a range of masses within the spring’s elastic limit
Use small vertical oscillations and a fixed reference marker
Time 10 or 20 complete oscillations; repeat, average and divide by the count
Plot T² against total suspended mass m
A straight line supports T² ∝ m; gradient = 4π²/k, so k = 4π²/gradient
Secure or weight the stand and keep clear of falling masses; do not overload the spring

questions.prompt: A cyclist rides 1.2 km due north in 4.0 minutes, then 0.50 km due east in 1.5 minutes. State the difference between distance and displacement.
scheme: B1 · Displacement is a vector (has a direction); distance is a scalar (magnitude only) / distance is measured along the path, displacement is the straight line from start to finish

questions.prompt: A cyclist rides 1.2 km due north in 4.0 minutes, then 0.50 km due east in 1.5 minutes. Calculate the average speed of the cyclist for the whole journey.
scheme: C1 · Total distance = 1700 m and total time = 330 s

numeric.hint: Convert km to m and minutes to s first.

questions.prompt: A cyclist rides 1.2 km due north in 4.0 minutes, then 0.50 km due east in 1.5 minutes. Calculate the magnitude of the cyclist’s displacement at the end of the journey and its direction as a bearing.
scheme: B1 · Angle = tan⁻¹(500 / 1200) = 23° east of north, i.e. bearing 023°

questions.prompt: A cyclist rides 1.2 km due north in 4.0 minutes, then 0.50 km due east in 1.5 minutes. Calculate the average velocity of the cyclist for the journey.
scheme: A1 · = 3.9 m s⁻¹ on a bearing of 023° (direction required)

questions.prompt: A train travels between two stations 36 km apart. The journey takes 25 minutes, including a stop at an intermediate station. The train’s maximum speed is 40 m s⁻¹. Define average speed.
scheme: B1 · Total distance travelled divided by the total time taken

questions.prompt: A train travels between two stations 36 km apart. The journey takes 25 minutes, including a stop at an intermediate station. The train’s maximum speed is 40 m s⁻¹. Calculate the average speed of the train in m s⁻¹.

A train travels between two stations 36 km apart. The journey takes 25 minutes, including a stop at an intermediate station. The train’s maximum speed is 40 m s⁻¹. Explain why the average speed is less than the maximum speed of 40 m s⁻¹.
scheme: B1 · The train accelerates, decelerates and is stationary at the stop, so for much of the journey its (instantaneous) speed is below 40 m s⁻¹
B1 · Average speed takes the whole time into account, including the time spent moving slowly or at rest

questions.prompt: Which of these is a vector quantity?
scheme: Displacement has a direction; the others are scalars.

questions.prompt: A car travels 30 km in 20 minutes. What is its average speed in m s⁻¹?
A walker goes 300 m east then 400 m north in 500 s. What is the magnitude of her average velocity?
scheme: Displacement = √(300² + 400²) = 500 m, so average velocity = 500/500 = 1.0 m s⁻¹ (bearing 037°). Her average speed is 700/500 = 1.4 m s⁻¹.

questions.prompt: When can the average speed equal the magnitude of the average velocity?
options: Only when the object moves in a straight line without reversing
Only when the speed is constant
scheme: Distance equals the size of the displacement only for straight-line motion in one direction.

questions.prompt: Convert 72 km h⁻¹ into m s⁻¹.
scheme: 72 000 m ÷ 3600 s = 20 m s⁻¹ (or divide by 3.6).

questions.prompt: A sports car accelerates from rest to 27 m s⁻¹ in 3.6 s. Define acceleration.
scheme: B1 · Rate of change of velocity (allow change in velocity ÷ time taken)

questions.prompt: A sports car accelerates from rest to 27 m s⁻¹ in 3.6 s. Calculate the average acceleration of the car.
A sports car accelerates from rest to 27 m s⁻¹ in 3.6 s. Express this acceleration as a multiple of g.
A sports car accelerates from rest to 27 m s⁻¹ in 3.6 s. The car later drives round a roundabout at a constant speed. Explain why the car is accelerating.
scheme: B1 · The direction of motion changes, so the velocity changes (velocity is a vector)
B1 · Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so a changing velocity means the car is accelerating

questions.prompt: A tennis ball travelling horizontally at 22 m s⁻¹ hits a wall and rebounds along the same line at 16 m s⁻¹. The ball is in contact with the wall for 0.040 s. Calculate the magnitude of the change in velocity of the ball.
scheme: C1 · Taking towards the wall as positive: Δv = (−16) − (+22)
A1 · |Δv| = 38 m s⁻¹ (away from the wall)

numeric.hint: The ball reverses direction, so the velocities have opposite signs.

questions.prompt: A tennis ball travelling horizontally at 22 m s⁻¹ hits a wall and rebounds along the same line at 16 m s⁻¹. The ball is in contact with the wall for 0.040 s. Calculate the magnitude of the average acceleration of the ball while it is in contact with the wall, and state its direction.
scheme: A1 · = 950 m s⁻², directed away from the wall

questions.prompt: A tennis ball travelling horizontally at 22 m s⁻¹ hits a wall and rebounds along the same line at 16 m s⁻¹. The ball is in contact with the wall for 0.040 s. A student calculates the acceleration as 150 m s⁻². Suggest the error the student has made.
scheme: B1 · Used the difference in speeds, 22 − 16 = 6 m s⁻¹, ignoring the change of direction

questions.prompt: A cyclist speeds up from 3.0 m s⁻¹ to 9.0 m s⁻¹ in 4.0 s. What is her acceleration?
A train has velocity +20 m s⁻¹ and acceleration −0.5 m s⁻². What happens?
scheme: Velocity and acceleration are in opposite directions, so the train slows down (by 0.5 m s⁻¹ every second).

questions.prompt: How long does it take an object to go from rest to 30 m s⁻¹ with an acceleration of 2.5 m s⁻²?
An object moving in the negative direction has a negative acceleration. It is…
scheme: Both vectors point the same way, so the speed increases.

questions.prompt: A car moving round a roundabout at a constant speed of 10 m s⁻¹ is…
options: not accelerating, because its speed is constant
accelerating, because its direction (and so velocity) is changing
scheme: Velocity is a vector; a change of direction is a change of velocity, so there is an acceleration (towards the centre).

questions.prompt: The graph shows how the displacement of a remote-controlled car changes with time.01234567891002468101214time / sdisplacement / m Describe the motion of the car between 0 and 10 s.
scheme: B1 · 0–4 s: moves away at a constant velocity (of 3.0 m s⁻¹)
B1 · 4–7 s: stationary (at 12 m from the start)
B1 · 7–10 s: returns to the start at a constant velocity (of 4.0 m s⁻¹) in the opposite direction

questions.prompt: The graph shows how the displacement of a remote-controlled car changes with time.01234567891002468101214time / sdisplacement / m Calculate the velocity of the car between 7 s and 10 s.
scheme: A1 · = −4.0 m s⁻¹ (allow 4.0 m s⁻¹ back towards the start)

numeric.hint: Gradient = change in displacement ÷ change in time. Think about the sign.

questions.prompt: The graph shows how the displacement of a remote-controlled car changes with time.01234567891002468101214time / sdisplacement / m Calculate the average speed and the average velocity of the car over the 10 s.
scheme: B1 · Average speed = 24 m / 10 s = 2.4 m s⁻¹
B1 · Average velocity = 0 (it finishes where it started)

questions.prompt: An object accelerates from rest. Its displacement–time graph is a curve. To find the velocity at t = 3.0 s, a student draws a tangent to the curve; the tangent passes through the points (1.5 s, 0 m) and (5.0 s, 12.6 m). Explain how the instantaneous velocity is found from a displacement–time graph.
scheme: B1 · Draw a tangent to the curve at the time required
B1 · Velocity = gradient of the tangent (Δs / Δt, using a large triangle)

questions.prompt: An object accelerates from rest. Its displacement–time graph is a curve. To find the velocity at t = 3.0 s, a student draws a tangent to the curve; the tangent passes through the points (1.5 s, 0 m) and (5.0 s, 12.6 m). Calculate the velocity of the object at t = 3.0 s.

An object accelerates from rest. Its displacement–time graph is a curve. To find the velocity at t = 3.0 s, a student draws a tangent to the curve; the tangent passes through the points (1.5 s, 0 m) and (5.0 s, 12.6 m). State how the displacement–time graph shows that the object is accelerating.
scheme: B1 · The gradient increases / the curve gets steeper with time

questions.prompt: On a displacement–time graph a straight line passes through (2 s, 5 m) and (6 s, 25 m). What is the velocity?
A displacement–time graph is a curve that gets less steep with time. The object is…
The tangent to an s–t curve at t = 5 s passes through (2 s, 4 m) and (8 s, 40 m). Find the instantaneous velocity at 5 s.
What does a section with a negative gradient on a displacement–time graph show?
options: The object is moving in the negative direction
The object is below the starting point
scheme: Negative gradient = negative velocity. Slowing down shows as a decreasing steepness instead.

questions.prompt: In the explorer journey the object returns from 60 m to 28 m between t = 17 s and t = 25 s. What is its velocity?

The velocity–time graph shows a car travelling between two sets of traffic lights. It accelerates uniformly from rest to 15 m s⁻¹ in 6.0 s, travels at constant velocity until t = 16 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest at t = 21 s.02468101214161820220369121518time / svelocity / m s⁻¹ Calculate the acceleration of the car during the first 6.0 s.

The velocity–time graph shows a car travelling between two sets of traffic lights. It accelerates uniformly from rest to 15 m s⁻¹ in 6.0 s, travels at constant velocity until t = 16 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest at t = 21 s.02468101214161820220369121518time / svelocity / m s⁻¹ Calculate the distance between the two sets of traffic lights.
scheme: C1 · Uses area under the graph

numeric.hint: Distance is the total area under the v–t graph.

questions.prompt: The velocity–time graph shows a car travelling between two sets of traffic lights. It accelerates uniformly from rest to 15 m s⁻¹ in 6.0 s, travels at constant velocity until t = 16 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest at t = 21 s.02468101214161820220369121518time / svelocity / m s⁻¹ Describe the acceleration–time graph for the 21 s journey, giving values.
scheme: B1 · 0–6 s: constant acceleration of 2.5 m s⁻²
B1 · 16–21 s: constant (negative) acceleration of −3.0 m s⁻²

questions.prompt: An object starts from rest. It accelerates at a constant 4.0 m s⁻² for 3.0 s and then moves with zero acceleration. State what is represented by the area under an acceleration–time graph.
An object starts from rest. It accelerates at a constant 4.0 m s⁻² for 3.0 s and then moves with zero acceleration. Calculate the velocity of the object after 3.0 s.

An object starts from rest. It accelerates at a constant 4.0 m s⁻² for 3.0 s and then moves with zero acceleration. A different object has a velocity–time graph with part of its area below the time axis. Explain what this area represents.
scheme: B1 · Velocity is negative, so the object is moving in the opposite (negative) direction
B1 · The area is the displacement in that direction; it is subtracted from the area above the axis to find the net displacement

questions.prompt: A v–t graph is a straight line from 4 m s⁻¹ at t = 0 to 16 m s⁻¹ at t = 6 s. What is the acceleration?
For the same graph (4 → 16 m s⁻¹ in 6 s), what is the displacement?
What does a horizontal line on a velocity–time graph mean?
scheme: Zero gradient means zero acceleration: the velocity is constant.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown up at 12 m s⁻¹ and caught at the same height. What is the total area (net displacement) under its v–t graph?
scheme: The positive area (going up) equals the negative area (coming down), so the net displacement is zero. The distance travelled is 2 × 7.3 = 14.7 m.

questions.prompt: An a–t graph shows a constant 2.5 m s⁻² for 4.0 s. What is the change in velocity?
scheme: Area under the a–t graph = 2.5 × 4.0 = 10 m s⁻¹.

m5.title: Linking displacement, velocity and acceleration graphs

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown vertically upwards and caught at the same height. Take upwards as positive and ignore air resistance. Describe the velocity–time graph for the ball’s motion from release until it is caught.
scheme: B1 · Gradient is negative and equal to −9.81 m s⁻² (−g)
B1 · Starts at a positive value, crosses zero at the top of the flight, and ends at a negative value of equal magnitude

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown vertically upwards and caught at the same height. Take upwards as positive and ignore air resistance. Describe the displacement–time graph for the same motion.
scheme: B1 · A symmetrical curve (inverted parabola) rising then falling back to zero
B1 · Maximum displacement (gradient zero) at the same time the velocity is zero

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown vertically upwards and caught at the same height. Take upwards as positive and ignore air resistance. Describe the acceleration–time graph.
scheme: B1 · A horizontal line at −9.81 m s⁻² throughout

questions.prompt: A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 1.8 m onto a hard floor and bounces. Which velocity–time graph corresponds to a displacement–time graph that is a straight line with a positive gradient?
options: A straight line through the origin with positive gradient
A horizontal line above the time axis
A horizontal line on the time axis
A straight line with negative gradient

questions.prompt: A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 1.8 m onto a hard floor and bounces. Calculate the speed of the ball just before it hits the floor.
A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 1.8 m onto a hard floor and bounces. On a velocity–time graph of the bounce, the lines before and after the impact are parallel. Explain why.
scheme: B1 · The gradient of a v–t graph is the acceleration
B1 · Before and after the bounce the only force is the weight, so the acceleration is g (same gradient) in both cases

questions.prompt: At the highest point of a ball thrown vertically upwards, which is true?
scheme: The ball is momentarily at rest, but gravity still acts so the acceleration is −9.81 m s⁻² (up positive).

questions.prompt: An s–t graph is a straight line with positive gradient. What does the a–t graph look like?
options: A straight line with positive gradient
scheme: Straight s–t ⇒ constant velocity ⇒ zero acceleration.

questions.prompt: A v–t graph is a horizontal line at −3 m s⁻¹. What does the s–t graph look like?
scheme: Constant negative velocity ⇒ displacement decreases steadily.

questions.prompt: For the lift, the acceleration is 1.0 m s⁻² for the first 2.0 s from rest. What is the velocity at 2.0 s?
Why is each bounce of the dropped ball lower than the last?
options: Kinetic energy is lost in each collision with the floor
scheme: Some kinetic energy is transferred to heat and sound on impact, so the ball leaves the floor slower than it arrived.

questions.prompt: The equations of motion can be derived from the definition of acceleration and the velocity–time graph for uniformly accelerated motion. State two conditions that must be met for the equations of motion to apply.
scheme: B1 · The motion is in a straight line

questions.prompt: The equations of motion can be derived from the definition of acceleration and the velocity–time graph for uniformly accelerated motion. Starting from the definition of acceleration, show that v = u + at.
scheme: B1 · a = (v − u) / t, rearranged to v = u + at

questions.prompt: The equations of motion can be derived from the definition of acceleration and the velocity–time graph for uniformly accelerated motion. Use the area under a velocity–time graph to show that s = ut + ½at².
scheme: B1 · Area under the graph = rectangle ut + triangle
B1 · Triangle area = ½ × t × (v − u)
B1 · Substitutes v − u = at to give s = ut + ½at²

questions.prompt: The equations of motion can be derived from the definition of acceleration and the velocity–time graph for uniformly accelerated motion. Use s = ½(u + v)t and v = u + at to derive v² = u² + 2as.
scheme: M1 · Substitutes t = (v − u) / a into s = ½(u + v)t
A1 · s = (v² − u²) / 2a, rearranged to v² = u² + 2as

questions.prompt: An equation is homogeneous if every term has the same base units. Show that the equation s = ut + ½at² is homogeneous.
scheme: B1 · ut: m s⁻¹ × s = m and ½at²: m s⁻² × s² = m
B1 · Every term (including s) has base unit m, so the equation is homogeneous

questions.prompt: An equation is homogeneous if every term has the same base units. Explain why showing that an equation is homogeneous does not prove that it is correct.
scheme: B1 · Dimensionless constants (such as the ½) cannot be checked / terms could be missing or wrong by a numerical factor

questions.prompt: Which equation does NOT contain the time t?
scheme: v² = u² + 2as is obtained by eliminating t.

questions.prompt: On a v–t graph for uniform acceleration, what does the term ½at² represent?
options: The rectangle under the initial velocity
The triangle above the initial velocity
scheme: The triangle has base t and height at, so its area is ½ × t × at = ½at².

questions.prompt: A car starts at 5.0 m s⁻¹ and accelerates at 2.0 m s⁻² for 4.0 s. Using s = ut + ½at², find s.
Which situation can be analysed with the suvat equations?
options: A ball rolling down a uniform slope with negligible friction
A car whose acceleration decreases as it speeds up
scheme: Only the ball on the slope has constant acceleration in a straight line.

m7.title: Solving problems with the equations of motion

questions.prompt: A train decelerates uniformly from 32 m s⁻¹ to rest over a distance of 640 m. Calculate the deceleration of the train.
scheme: A1 · a = −0.80 m s⁻² (deceleration 0.80 m s⁻²)

questions.prompt: A train decelerates uniformly from 32 m s⁻¹ to rest over a distance of 640 m. Calculate the time taken for the train to stop.
A train decelerates uniformly from 32 m s⁻¹ to rest over a distance of 640 m. Calculate the distance travelled by the train in the final 10 s before it stops.
scheme: C1 · Speed 10 s before stopping = 0.80 × 10 = 8.0 m s⁻¹

numeric.hint: Find the speed 10 s before it stops, or work backwards from rest.

questions.prompt: Car A travels along a straight road at a constant 20 m s⁻¹. As it passes car B, car B starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2.5 m s⁻² in the same direction. Calculate the time taken for car B to catch up with car A.

Car A travels along a straight road at a constant 20 m s⁻¹. As it passes car B, car B starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2.5 m s⁻² in the same direction. Calculate the distance travelled by car B in this time.

Car A travels along a straight road at a constant 20 m s⁻¹. As it passes car B, car B starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2.5 m s⁻² in the same direction. Calculate the speed of car B as it passes car A.
A ball is dropped from a height of 20 m. Taking g = 9.81 m s⁻², how long does it take to reach the ground?
A car accelerates from rest at 3.0 m s⁻² over 150 m. What is its final speed?
A train slows from 40 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹ in 25 s. How far does it travel in that time?
'A ball is thrown vertically upwards and reaches its maximum height.' Which value is implied?
scheme: At the top the ball is momentarily at rest, so v = 0. The acceleration is still −g.

questions.prompt: A stone is dropped from rest from the top of a cliff. It hits the sea 3.2 s later. Ignore air resistance. Calculate the height of the cliff.
A stone is dropped from rest from the top of a cliff. It hits the sea 3.2 s later. Ignore air resistance. Calculate the speed of the stone as it hits the sea.
A stone is dropped from rest from the top of a cliff. It hits the sea 3.2 s later. Ignore air resistance. In reality, the stone takes slightly longer than 3.2 s to fall this height. Explain why.
scheme: B1 · Air resistance acts upwards, so the resultant force and hence the acceleration are less than g

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 14 m s⁻¹ from a point 1.5 m above the ground. Ignore air resistance. Calculate the maximum height of the ball above the ground.
scheme: C1 · 0 = 14² − 2 × 9.81 × s, so s = 10.0 m above the release point

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 14 m s⁻¹ from a point 1.5 m above the ground. Ignore air resistance. Calculate the time from release until the ball hits the ground.
scheme: C1 · Solves 4.905t² − 14t − 1.5 = 0 using the quadratic formula

numeric.hint: The displacement is −1.5 m (taking up as positive). You need the quadratic formula.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 14 m s⁻¹ from a point 1.5 m above the ground. Ignore air resistance. State why the mass of the ball does not affect your answers.
scheme: B1 · All objects in free fall (no air resistance) have the same acceleration g, whatever their mass

questions.prompt: A hammer and a feather are dropped together on the Moon (no atmosphere). Which lands first?
scheme: With no air resistance both accelerate at the Moon's free-fall acceleration, 1.6 m s⁻², whatever their mass. Astronaut David Scott did exactly this on Apollo 15.

questions.prompt: A stone is dropped from rest. How fast is it moving after 1.5 s? (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
A ball is thrown upwards at 15 m s⁻¹. How long does it take to reach the top?
Taking up as positive, what is the acceleration of a ball at the top of its flight?
scheme: Gravity still acts downwards: a = −9.81 m s⁻² throughout the flight.

questions.prompt: A ball thrown upwards returns to the thrower's hand. How does its speed when caught compare with the launch speed (no air resistance)?
scheme: The motion is symmetric: it returns at the same speed, in the opposite direction.

m9.title: Determining the acceleration of free fall

questions.prompt: A student drops a steel ball from an electromagnet through different heights h onto a trapdoor. An electronic timer measures the fall time t. She plots a graph of h against t². The best-fit line has gradient 4.86 m s⁻² and the worst acceptable line has gradient 5.02 m s⁻². The best-fit line cuts the t² axis at a small positive value. Show that the gradient of the graph is equal to g/2.
scheme: B1 · h = ½gt² (u = 0), which has the form y = mx with y = h, x = t² and m = g/2

A sledge of mass 25 kg slides down a straight slope inclined at 20° to the horizontal. The frictional force on the sledge is 30 N.20° Calculate the normal contact force on the sledge.
A sledge of mass 25 kg slides down a straight slope inclined at 20° to the horizontal. The frictional force on the sledge is 30 N.20° Calculate the acceleration of the sledge down the slope.
scheme: C1 · Resultant force down the slope = 83.9 − 30 = 53.9 N

questions.prompt: A sledge of mass 25 kg slides down a straight slope inclined at 20° to the horizontal. The frictional force on the sledge is 30 N.20° The angle of the slope is increased. State and explain the effect on the normal contact force.
scheme: B1 · It decreases, because N = mg cos θ and cos θ decreases as θ increases

questions.prompt: A crate of mass 20 kg rests on a smooth horizontal floor. A rope pulls the crate with a force of 50 N at 30° above the horizontal. Calculate the horizontal component of the pull.
A crate of mass 20 kg rests on a smooth horizontal floor. A rope pulls the crate with a force of 50 N at 30° above the horizontal. Calculate the acceleration of the crate.
A crate of mass 20 kg rests on a smooth horizontal floor. A rope pulls the crate with a force of 50 N at 30° above the horizontal. Calculate the normal contact force of the floor on the crate.

numeric.hint: The rope pulls partly upwards, so the floor supports less than the full weight.

questions.prompt: A 50 N force acts at 40° above the horizontal. What is its horizontal component?
…and its vertical component?
A frictionless trolley rolls down a 12° slope. What is its acceleration?
scheme: a = g sin θ = 9.81 sin 12° = 2.04 m s⁻².

questions.prompt: A 2.0 kg box rests on a 20° slope without sliding. What friction force acts on it?
scheme: Friction balances the component down the slope: 2.0 × 9.81 × sin 20° = 6.71 N up the slope.

questions.prompt: As the angle of a slope increases, the normal contact force on a block…
scheme: R = mg cos θ, and cos θ decreases as θ increases.

questions.prompt: A person of mass 70 kg stands on bathroom scales in a lift. The scales measure the normal contact force on the person. Calculate the reading on the scales when the lift accelerates upwards at 1.5 m s⁻².
A person of mass 70 kg stands on bathroom scales in a lift. The scales measure the normal contact force on the person. Calculate the reading when the lift moves upwards at a constant speed.

A person of mass 70 kg stands on bathroom scales in a lift. The scales measure the normal contact force on the person. The cable breaks and the lift falls freely. Explain why the person feels weightless.
scheme: B1 · The person and the lift both accelerate downwards at g
B1 · The weight alone provides the resultant force, so the normal contact force (the scale reading) is zero

questions.prompt: A car of mass 1500 kg tows a trailer of mass 500 kg along a straight, horizontal road. The resistive forces are 400 N on the car and 200 N on the trailer. The car and trailer accelerate at 0.80 m s⁻². Calculate the driving force on the car.
scheme: C1 · For the whole system: F − 600 = 2000 × 0.80

questions.prompt: A car of mass 1500 kg tows a trailer of mass 500 kg along a straight, horizontal road. The resistive forces are 400 N on the car and 200 N on the trailer. The car and trailer accelerate at 0.80 m s⁻². Calculate the tension in the tow bar.

numeric.hint: Apply F = ma to the trailer on its own.

questions.prompt: A car of mass 1500 kg tows a trailer of mass 500 kg along a straight, horizontal road. The resistive forces are 400 N on the car and 200 N on the trailer. The car and trailer accelerate at 0.80 m s⁻². The tow bar breaks and the driving force stays the same. What is the acceleration of the car immediately afterwards?
A 50 kg person is in a lift accelerating downwards at 2.0 m s⁻². What force do the scales exert?
A lift moves upwards at a constant 3 m s⁻¹. The scale reading is…
Why do astronauts in the orbiting International Space Station feel weightless?
options: There is no gravity in space
They and the station are both in free fall
scheme: g at that height is still about 8.7 N kg⁻¹; they and the station fall together, so there is no contact force between them.

questions.prompt: A 3.0 kg trolley is pulled by a 1.0 kg hanging mass over a smooth pulley. What is the acceleration?
…and the tension in the string?
scheme: T = 3.0 × 2.45 = 7.36 N (less than the hanging weight of 9.81 N).

questions.prompt: A cyclist travels along a flat road. The drag force D on the cyclist is given by D = kv², where k = 0.25 kg m⁻¹. State what is meant by drag.
scheme: B1 · The resistive (frictional) force on an object moving through a fluid, opposing its motion

questions.prompt: A cyclist travels along a flat road. The drag force D on the cyclist is given by D = kv², where k = 0.25 kg m⁻¹. State two factors, other than speed, that affect the drag on the cyclist.
scheme: B1 · Cross-sectional area / shape (streamlining) of the cyclist
B1 · Density (or viscosity) of the air / roughness of the surface

questions.prompt: A cyclist travels along a flat road. The drag force D on the cyclist is given by D = kv², where k = 0.25 kg m⁻¹. Calculate the drag on the cyclist at 12 m s⁻¹.

A cyclist travels along a flat road. The drag force D on the cyclist is given by D = kv², where k = 0.25 kg m⁻¹. The cyclist provides a constant forward force of 60 N. Calculate the maximum speed the cyclist can reach.
A car starts from rest and its engine provides a constant driving force. Explain why the acceleration of the car decreases as its speed increases.
scheme: B1 · Drag (air resistance) increases with speed
B1 · So the resultant force (driving force − drag) decreases
B1 · a = F/m, so the acceleration decreases (reaching zero at the maximum speed)

questions.prompt: A car starts from rest and its engine provides a constant driving force. The drag on an object is proportional to v². By what factor does the drag change when the speed doubles?
Drag on a car is proportional to v². By what factor does the drag increase when its speed rises from 15 m s⁻¹ to 30 m s⁻¹?
Which change reduces the drag on a cyclist at the same speed?
scheme: Crouching reduces the cross-sectional area and improves streamlining.

questions.prompt: Why does a swimmer experience much more drag than a runner at the same speed?
options: Water is denser and more viscous than air
scheme: Drag increases with the density (and viscosity) of the fluid.

questions.prompt: A car's drag is 600 N at 20 m s⁻¹ (D ∝ v²). What is the drag at 25 m s⁻¹?

A skydiver of mass 80 kg jumps from a hovering helicopter and reaches a terminal velocity of 55 m s⁻¹. She then opens her parachute. Explain, in terms of the forces on her, why the skydiver reaches a terminal velocity.
scheme: B1 · At first the only force is her weight, so she accelerates at g
B1 · As her speed increases the drag increases, so the resultant force and the acceleration decrease
B1 · When the drag equals the weight the resultant force is zero and the velocity is constant

questions.prompt: A skydiver of mass 80 kg jumps from a hovering helicopter and reaches a terminal velocity of 55 m s⁻¹. She then opens her parachute. Calculate the drag on the skydiver at terminal velocity.

A skydiver of mass 80 kg jumps from a hovering helicopter and reaches a terminal velocity of 55 m s⁻¹. She then opens her parachute. Just after the parachute opens the drag is 2400 N. Calculate the magnitude of her deceleration.

A skydiver of mass 80 kg jumps from a hovering helicopter and reaches a terminal velocity of 55 m s⁻¹. She then opens her parachute. Describe the velocity–time graph from the moment the parachute opens until she reaches her new terminal velocity.
scheme: B1 · Velocity falls steeply at first (large negative gradient)
B1 · The gradient decreases to zero as the velocity levels off at a lower terminal velocity

questions.prompt: A student drops a steel ball bearing into a tall tube of glycerol. Rubber bands are placed around the tube at intervals of 10.0 cm. Describe how the student could check that the ball has reached terminal velocity.
scheme: B1 · Time the ball between successive pairs of bands
B1 · Terminal velocity is reached when the times between equally spaced bands are the same

questions.prompt: A student drops a steel ball bearing into a tall tube of glycerol. Rubber bands are placed around the tube at intervals of 10.0 cm. The ball takes 0.80 s to travel between two bands once it is at terminal velocity. Calculate the terminal velocity.

A student drops a steel ball bearing into a tall tube of glycerol. Rubber bands are placed around the tube at intervals of 10.0 cm. Suggest one way of reducing the percentage uncertainty in the time measurement.
scheme: B1 · Increase the distance between the bands / film with a video camera and use frame-by-frame playback / repeat and average

questions.prompt: At the instant a ball is dropped from rest in air, its acceleration is…
scheme: v = 0 so there is no drag yet; the only force is the weight.

questions.prompt: A 60 kg skydiver falls at terminal velocity. What is the drag force?
scheme: At terminal velocity D = W = 60 × 9.81 = 589 N.

questions.prompt: Just after a parachute opens, the skydiver…
scheme: Drag exceeds weight, so the resultant force (and acceleration) is upwards, but the velocity is still downwards: she slows down.

questions.prompt: A 0.050 kg object falling in air experiences a drag of 0.30 N. What is its acceleration?
How can you tell from equal-interval timings that a ball in glycerol has reached terminal velocity?
options: The times between bands are equal
scheme: Equal distances in equal times means constant velocity.

f7.title: Moments and the principle of moments

questions.prompt: A uniform plank of length 4.0 m and weight 200 N rests on two supports. Support A is at one end and support B is 1.0 m from the other end. A child of weight 300 N stands 1.0 m from A.ABchild1.0 m1.0 m4.0 m plank Define the moment of a force about a point.
scheme: B1 · Force × perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force

questions.prompt: A uniform plank of length 4.0 m and weight 200 N rests on two supports. Support A is at one end and support B is 1.0 m from the other end. A child of weight 300 N stands 1.0 m from A.ABchild1.0 m1.0 m4.0 m plank State the principle of moments.
scheme: B1 · For an object in (rotational) equilibrium
B1 · the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point

questions.prompt: A uniform plank of length 4.0 m and weight 200 N rests on two supports. Support A is at one end and support B is 1.0 m from the other end. A child of weight 300 N stands 1.0 m from A.ABchild1.0 m1.0 m4.0 m plank Calculate the force exerted on the plank by support B.

numeric.hint: Take moments about A. The plank’s weight acts at its centre, 2.0 m from A.

questions.prompt: A uniform plank of length 4.0 m and weight 200 N rests on two supports. Support A is at one end and support B is 1.0 m from the other end. A child of weight 300 N stands 1.0 m from A.ABchild1.0 m1.0 m4.0 m plank Calculate the force exerted on the plank by support A.

A mechanic tightens a nut using a spanner. She applies a force of 40 N at a distance of 0.25 m from the centre of the nut. Calculate the moment about the nut when the force is perpendicular to the spanner.

A mechanic tightens a nut using a spanner. She applies a force of 40 N at a distance of 0.25 m from the centre of the nut. She now applies the 40 N force at the same point but at 60° to the spanner. Calculate the new moment.
scheme: C1 · Perpendicular distance = 0.25 sin 60° (or perpendicular component of force = 40 sin 60°)

questions.prompt: A 30 N force acts at right angles to a spanner, 0.25 m from the nut. What is its moment?
A 400 N child sits 1.5 m from the pivot of a see-saw. How far from the pivot on the other side must a 600 N adult sit to balance?
A 20 N force acts at 30° to a lever, 0.40 m from the pivot. What is its moment?
scheme: Perpendicular component: 20 sin 30° = 10 N; moment = 10 × 0.40 = 4.0 N m.

questions.prompt: A uniform 1.0 m rule weighing 1.2 N is pivoted at the 30 cm mark. What mass, hung at the 10 cm mark, balances it?
scheme: Weight acts at 50 cm: 1.2 × 0.20 = 0.24 N m clockwise. Load at 0.20 m left: F = 0.24/0.20 = 1.2 N ⇒ m = 1.2/9.81 = 0.12 kg.

questions.prompt: For a body to be in equilibrium, which conditions must hold?
options: Both resultant force and resultant moment zero
The body must be at rest
scheme: Both are needed; a body in equilibrium can still be moving at constant velocity.

f8.title: Couples and the torque of a couple

questions.prompt: A driver turns a steering wheel of diameter 0.38 m by applying two equal and opposite forces of 25 N, tangential to the rim, at opposite ends of a diameter. State what is meant by a couple.
scheme: B1 · A pair of equal and opposite (coplanar) forces whose lines of action are separated by a perpendicular distance

questions.prompt: A driver turns a steering wheel of diameter 0.38 m by applying two equal and opposite forces of 25 N, tangential to the rim, at opposite ends of a diameter. Calculate the torque of the couple.
scheme: C1 · Torque = one force × perpendicular separation of the forces

questions.prompt: A driver turns a steering wheel of diameter 0.38 m by applying two equal and opposite forces of 25 N, tangential to the rim, at opposite ends of a diameter. Explain why a couple makes the wheel rotate but does not make it move from side to side.
scheme: B1 · The forces are equal and opposite, so the resultant force is zero (no linear acceleration)
B1 · Their moments act in the same sense, so there is a resultant moment (torque) that causes rotation

questions.prompt: A rigid body is acted on by several coplanar forces. State the two conditions for the body to be in equilibrium.
scheme: B1 · The resultant force is zero (in every direction)
B1 · The resultant moment about any point is zero

questions.prompt: A rigid body is acted on by several coplanar forces. A couple consists of two forces of 8.0 N whose lines of action are 0.15 m apart. What is its torque?
Two forces of 25 N form a couple. Their lines of action are 0.40 m apart. What is the torque?
What is the resultant force produced by a couple?
scheme: The forces are equal and opposite, so they cancel.

questions.prompt: A driver applies 15 N tangentially at opposite sides of a steering wheel of diameter 0.38 m. What is the torque?
If the same forces act at 60° to the tangent instead, the torque…
scheme: The perpendicular separation becomes d cos 60° = d/2, so the torque halves.

f9.title: Centre of mass and centre of gravity

questions.prompt: A student needs to find the centre of gravity of a thin, irregularly shaped piece of card. Define centre of gravity.
scheme: B1 · The point through which the (whole) weight of an object appears to act

questions.prompt: A student needs to find the centre of gravity of a thin, irregularly shaped piece of card. Describe how the student could find the centre of gravity of the card.
scheme: B1 · Make a small hole near the edge and hang the card freely from a pin held in a clamp
B1 · Hang a plumb line from the pin and mark its line on the card
B1 · Repeat with the card hung from a second hole at a different point
B1 · The centre of gravity is where the lines cross (check with a third hole)

questions.prompt: A student needs to find the centre of gravity of a thin, irregularly shaped piece of card. Explain why a freely hanging card comes to rest with its centre of gravity directly below the pivot.
scheme: B1 · Only then does the weight act through the pivot, so it has no moment (no turning effect)

questions.prompt: A tall, uniform cabinet stands on a level floor. Its base is 0.60 m wide and its centre of gravity is 0.90 m above the floor, above the centre of the base. The cabinet is tilted about one bottom edge. Calculate the angle through which the cabinet can be tilted before it topples.
scheme: C1 · Topples when the centre of gravity is directly above the edge: tan θ = 0.30 / 0.90

questions.prompt: A tall, uniform cabinet stands on a level floor. Its base is 0.60 m wide and its centre of gravity is 0.90 m above the floor, above the centre of the base. The cabinet is tilted about one bottom edge. Explain why the cabinet topples if it is tilted beyond this angle.
scheme: B1 · The line of action of the weight falls outside the base (beyond the edge it pivots about)
B1 · The weight then has a moment about the edge in the direction of tipping, not a restoring moment

questions.prompt: A tall, uniform cabinet stands on a level floor. Its base is 0.60 m wide and its centre of gravity is 0.90 m above the floor, above the centre of the base. The cabinet is tilted about one bottom edge. Which change would make the cabinet more stable?
options: Putting heavy items in the bottom drawers

questions.prompt: Where is the centre of gravity of a uniform metre rule?
scheme: A uniform object's centre of gravity is at its geometric centre.

questions.prompt: Why does a lamina hanging freely from a pin come to rest with its centre of gravity directly below the pin?
options: Only then does its weight have no moment about the pin
scheme: If the centre of gravity were to one side, the weight would have a moment about the pin and the lamina would rotate.

questions.prompt: A block has a base 0.60 m wide and its centre of gravity is 0.80 m above the base. At what tilt angle does it topple?
Which change makes a vehicle LESS likely to topple on a slope?
options: Carrying passengers on the top deck
scheme: A wider base increases the tipping angle; the others raise the centre of gravity.

f10.title: Three forces in equilibrium: the triangle of forces

questions.prompt: A picture of weight 30 N hangs from a nail by a string. The two halves of the string are symmetrical and each makes an angle of 40° with the horizontal. Explain why the three forces on the picture can be drawn as a closed triangle.
scheme: B1 · The picture is in equilibrium, so the resultant force is zero
B1 · So the force vectors drawn tip-to-tail end where they started (a closed triangle)

questions.prompt: A picture of weight 30 N hangs from a nail by a string. The two halves of the string are symmetrical and each makes an angle of 40° with the horizontal. Calculate the tension in each half of the string.

A picture of weight 30 N hangs from a nail by a string. The two halves of the string are symmetrical and each makes an angle of 40° with the horizontal. Explain why the string is more likely to break if it is shortened so that each half makes a smaller angle with the horizontal.
scheme: B1 · The vertical components of the tensions must still add up to 30 N
B1 · A smaller angle means a smaller sin θ, so a larger tension is needed

questions.prompt: A lamp of weight 40 N hangs from a point where two cables meet. One cable is horizontal and is attached to a wall. The other cable makes an angle of 50° with the horizontal and is attached to the ceiling. Calculate the tension in the angled cable.

A lamp of weight 40 N hangs from a point where two cables meet. One cable is horizontal and is attached to a wall. The other cable makes an angle of 50° with the horizontal and is attached to the ceiling. Calculate the tension in the horizontal cable.
Three forces in equilibrium are drawn tip to tail. What shape do they make?
scheme: The resultant is zero, so the arrows end where they started.

questions.prompt: A 20 N picture hangs from a wire; both halves make 30° with the horizontal. What is the tension in the wire?
A 10 N weight hangs from two strings at 90° to each other. One string makes 60° with the horizontal. What is the tension in that string?
scheme: Right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 10 N: T = 10 sin 60° = 8.66 N (the other is 10 cos 60° = 5 N).

questions.prompt: Why is it impossible to pull a washing line perfectly straight when clothes hang from it?
options: The vertical components of tension would be zero, so they could not support the weight
scheme: Supporting the weight needs a vertical component 2T sin θ; as θ → 0, T → infinity.

questions.prompt: A student measures the density of an irregularly shaped stone. Its mass is 156 g. When it is lowered into a measuring cylinder of water, the water level rises from 50.0 cm³ to 110.0 cm³. Define density.
scheme: B1 · Mass per unit volume (ρ = m / V)

questions.prompt: A student measures the density of an irregularly shaped stone. Its mass is 156 g. When it is lowered into a measuring cylinder of water, the water level rises from 50.0 cm³ to 110.0 cm³. Calculate the density of the stone in kg m⁻³.

numeric.hint: 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³.

questions.prompt: A student measures the density of an irregularly shaped stone. Its mass is 156 g. When it is lowered into a measuring cylinder of water, the water level rises from 50.0 cm³ to 110.0 cm³. Suggest why this method may give a large uncertainty in the volume, and how it could be improved.
scheme: B1 · The scale divisions of a measuring cylinder are large compared with the volume measured / the meniscus is hard to read
B1 · Use a displacement (eureka) can and collect the water in a smaller measuring cylinder / read at eye level / use a larger sample

questions.prompt: A copper wire is 2.0 m long and has a diameter of 0.50 mm. The density of copper is 8900 kg m⁻³. Calculate the mass of the wire.

numeric.hint: Find the cross-sectional area πr² in m² first.

questions.prompt: A copper wire is 2.0 m long and has a diameter of 0.50 mm. The density of copper is 8900 kg m⁻³. A density of 1 g cm⁻³ is equal to
A block measures 5.0 cm × 4.0 cm × 2.0 cm and has a mass of 108 g. What is its density in g cm⁻³?
Convert 0.92 g cm⁻³ to kg m⁻³.
A stone is lowered into a measuring cylinder and the water level rises from 40 cm³ to 52 cm³. The stone's mass is 31.2 g. What is its density?
What is the mass of 2.0 m³ of air of density 1.2 kg m⁻³?
A diver is 25 m below the surface of the sea. The density of seawater is 1030 kg m⁻³ and atmospheric pressure is 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa. Define pressure.
scheme: B1 · Normal force per unit area

questions.prompt: A diver is 25 m below the surface of the sea. The density of seawater is 1030 kg m⁻³ and atmospheric pressure is 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa. Show that the pressure due to a column of liquid of height h and density ρ is p = hρg.
scheme: B1 · Consider a column of cross-sectional area A: volume = Ah
B1 · Mass = ρAh, so weight = ρAhg
B1 · p = weight / area = ρAhg / A = hρg

questions.prompt: A diver is 25 m below the surface of the sea. The density of seawater is 1030 kg m⁻³ and atmospheric pressure is 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate the pressure due to the water at the diver’s depth.
A diver is 25 m below the surface of the sea. The density of seawater is 1030 kg m⁻³ and atmospheric pressure is 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate the total pressure on the diver.

An elephant of mass 4000 kg stands with its weight spread evenly over four feet, each of area 0.10 m². A person of mass 60 kg balances her whole weight on one shoe heel of area 1.0 cm². Calculate the pressure under the elephant’s feet.

An elephant of mass 4000 kg stands with its weight spread evenly over four feet, each of area 0.10 m². A person of mass 60 kg balances her whole weight on one shoe heel of area 1.0 cm². Calculate the pressure under the heel.

An elephant of mass 4000 kg stands with its weight spread evenly over four feet, each of area 0.10 m². A person of mass 60 kg balances her whole weight on one shoe heel of area 1.0 cm². Three containers of different shapes are filled with water to the same depth. Where is the pressure at the bottom greatest?
options: It is the same in all three
In the container holding the most water

questions.prompt: A 600 N person stands on one foot of area 0.015 m². What pressure do they exert on the floor?
What is the pressure due to water at a depth of 4.0 m?
A mercury barometer column is 0.760 m high (ρ = 13 600 kg m⁻³). What pressure does it show?
Three vessels of different shapes are filled with water to the same depth. The pressure at the bottom is…
options: greatest in the one holding most water
scheme: p = hρg depends only on depth, density and g.

questions.prompt: At what depth in olive oil (ρ = 910 kg m⁻³) is the pressure due to the oil 5000 Pa?
A rectangular block of wood measures 0.20 m × 0.10 m × 0.050 m and has a density of 600 kg m⁻³. It is placed in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³ and floats. State Archimedes’ principle.
scheme: B1 · The upthrust on an object in a fluid equals the weight of fluid it displaces

questions.prompt: A rectangular block of wood measures 0.20 m × 0.10 m × 0.050 m and has a density of 600 kg m⁻³. It is placed in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³ and floats. Explain, in terms of pressure, why there is an upthrust on the block.
scheme: B1 · Pressure in a fluid increases with depth
B1 · So the pressure on the bottom face is greater than on the top face, giving a net upward force

questions.prompt: A rectangular block of wood measures 0.20 m × 0.10 m × 0.050 m and has a density of 600 kg m⁻³. It is placed in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³ and floats. Calculate the weight of the block.

A rectangular block of wood measures 0.20 m × 0.10 m × 0.050 m and has a density of 600 kg m⁻³. It is placed in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³ and floats. Calculate the volume of the block below the surface of the water.
scheme: C1 · Floating: upthrust = weight, so 1000 × V × 9.81 = 5.886

questions.prompt: A metal sphere of volume 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³ and weight 15 N hangs from a newton meter. The sphere is fully submerged in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. Calculate the upthrust on the sphere.
A metal sphere of volume 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³ and weight 15 N hangs from a newton meter. The sphere is fully submerged in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. Calculate the reading on the newton meter.

A metal sphere of volume 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³ and weight 15 N hangs from a newton meter. The sphere is fully submerged in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. The sphere is lowered deeper, but stays fully submerged. What happens to the upthrust?
A 0.50 m³ object is fully submerged in water. What is the upthrust on it?
An object weighs 12.0 N in air and 7.5 N when fully submerged in water. What is its volume?
A block of wood of density 600 kg m⁻³ floats in water. What fraction of its volume is under the water?
A ship sails from fresh water into denser sea water. It…
scheme: Upthrust must still equal its weight; denser water means less volume needs to be displaced, so it floats higher.

questions.prompt: Why does upthrust act upwards?
options: The pressure on the bottom of the object is greater than on the top
scheme: Pressure increases with depth, so the upward force on the lower surface exceeds the downward force on the upper surface.

f14.title: Forces in action: review and exam practice

questions.prompt: A crate of mass 40 kg is pulled up a rough slope inclined at 25° to the horizontal by a rope parallel to the slope. The frictional force on the crate is 80 N. Calculate the component of the crate’s weight acting down the slope.

A crate of mass 40 kg is pulled up a rough slope inclined at 25° to the horizontal by a rope parallel to the slope. The frictional force on the crate is 80 N. The crate moves up the slope at a constant speed. Calculate the tension in the rope.
scheme: C1 · Resultant force is zero, so T = mg sin θ + friction

questions.prompt: A crate of mass 40 kg is pulled up a rough slope inclined at 25° to the horizontal by a rope parallel to the slope. The frictional force on the crate is 80 N. The tension is increased to 300 N. Calculate the acceleration of the crate.

A crate of mass 40 kg is pulled up a rough slope inclined at 25° to the horizontal by a rope parallel to the slope. The frictional force on the crate is 80 N. The rope breaks while the crate is moving up the slope at 2.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the magnitude of the deceleration of the crate while it continues up the slope.
scheme: C1 · Resultant force down the slope = 166 + 80 = 246 N

numeric.hint: While the crate moves up, friction acts down the slope as well.

questions.prompt: A crate of mass 40 kg is pulled up a rough slope inclined at 25° to the horizontal by a rope parallel to the slope. The frictional force on the crate is 80 N. Calculate how far the crate travels up the slope after the rope breaks.

A crate of mass 40 kg is pulled up a rough slope inclined at 25° to the horizontal by a rope parallel to the slope. The frictional force on the crate is 80 N. The maximum frictional force between the crate and the slope is 80 N. Explain whether the crate slides back down the slope.
scheme: B1 · The component of the weight down the slope (166 N) is greater than the maximum friction (80 N)
B1 · So there is a resultant force down the slope (86 N) and the crate accelerates back down (at about 2.1 m s⁻²)

questions.prompt: A 1500 kg car accelerates at 2.4 m s⁻² against total resistive forces of 800 N. What is the driving force?
Which unit is equivalent to the newton?
scheme: F = ma ⇒ kg m s⁻². (J m⁻¹ is also equivalent, not J m.)

questions.prompt: A 12 kg box slides down a frictionless slope inclined at 25°. What is its acceleration?
scheme: a = g sin 25° = 4.15 m s⁻² (mass cancels).

questions.prompt: A 65 kg person stands in a lift decelerating at 1.5 m s⁻² while moving upwards. What force does the floor exert?
scheme: Acceleration is −1.5 m s⁻² (up positive): R = 65(9.81 − 1.5) = 540 N.

questions.prompt: A skydiver falls at terminal velocity. Which statement is correct?
scheme: Zero acceleration ⇒ zero resultant ⇒ D = W.

questions.prompt: A uniform 3.0 m plank weighing 150 N is supported at its ends. A 600 N person stands 1.0 m from the left end. What force does the right support provide?
scheme: Moments about the left end: R × 3.0 = 600 × 1.0 + 150 × 1.5 = 825 ⇒ R = 275 N. (The left support provides 750 − 275 = 475 N.)

questions.prompt: Two parallel forces of 8.0 N in opposite directions act on a disc, their lines of action 0.15 m apart. What is the torque?

scheme: C1 · Upthrust = Δp × area of face = 981 × 0.010

A student wants to determine the terminal velocity of a steel ball bearing falling through glycerol, and to show that the ball really has reached terminal velocity. Describe how the student could carry out the experiment and analyse the results. Include how the student would improve the accuracy of the measurements.
levels: Level 3 (5–6)

A clear method that would work, including how distance and time are measured at several points down the tube. Uses the data to show that terminal velocity has been reached and calculates its value. At least two sensible steps to improve accuracy. The answer is well structured with relevant detail.
Level 2 (3–4)
A workable method with some detail of measurements, and an attempt to find the terminal velocity. At least one step to improve accuracy. Some structure, though detail may be missing.
Level 1 (1–2)
A limited method or limited analysis. Information is basic and may be poorly organised.
No response or no response worthy of credit.
indicative: Fill a tall tube with glycerol; place rubber bands around the tube at equal measured intervals (e.g. 10.0 cm) using a metre rule
Release the ball from rest just at the surface, at the centre of the tube
Use a stopwatch, or film with a video camera beside a scale, to record the time at which the ball passes each band
Calculate the time for each interval; the ball has reached terminal velocity when the times between bands become constant
Terminal velocity = interval distance ÷ time (or the gradient of a distance–time graph once it becomes straight)

Accuracy: repeat with identical balls and average; read bands at eye level to avoid parallax; use larger band separations lower down; use video playback frame by frame; allow the first bands to be well below the surface; keep the temperature of the glycerol constant

ep1.title: Work done and conservation of energy

questions.prompt: A crate is dragged 20 m across a horizontal floor at constant speed by a rope inclined at 40° to the horizontal. The tension in the rope is 150 N. Define work done by a force.
scheme: B1 · Force × distance moved in the direction of the force

questions.prompt: A crate is dragged 20 m across a horizontal floor at constant speed by a rope inclined at 40° to the horizontal. The tension in the rope is 150 N. Calculate the work done by the tension.
scheme: C1 · W = Fx cos θ = 150 × 20 × cos 40°

questions.prompt: A crate is dragged 20 m across a horizontal floor at constant speed by a rope inclined at 40° to the horizontal. The tension in the rope is 150 N. Explain why the normal contact force from the floor does no work on the crate.
scheme: B1 · It acts at 90° to the displacement, so cos 90° = 0 / there is no movement in the direction of the force

questions.prompt: A crate is dragged 20 m across a horizontal floor at constant speed by a rope inclined at 40° to the horizontal. The tension in the rope is 150 N. Calculate the frictional force on the crate.
scheme: B1 · Constant speed, so friction = 150 cos 40° = 115 N

questions.prompt: A force of 25 N pushes a box 4.0 m along the floor in the direction of the force. How much work is done?
A rope with tension 50 N at 30° above the horizontal drags a crate 12 m across a floor. How much work is done by the tension?
A climber of mass 60 kg climbs 15 m vertically. How much work does she do against gravity? (g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹)
How much work is done by the centripetal force on a satellite in a circular orbit during one orbit?
options: Fx, where x is the circumference
It depends on the orbital speed
scheme: The force is always perpendicular to the motion (θ = 90°), so W = Fx cos 90° = 0.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the joule in SI base units?
scheme: J = N m = (kg m s⁻²) × m.

questions.prompt: A pendulum bob of mass 0.20 kg is pulled aside so that it is 0.15 m above its lowest point, and released from rest. Calculate the speed of the bob as it passes through its lowest point. Ignore air resistance.

A pendulum bob of mass 0.20 kg is pulled aside so that it is 0.15 m above its lowest point, and released from rest. Starting from W = Fx and an equation of motion, show that the kinetic energy of an object of mass m moving at speed v is ½mv².
scheme: M1 · A constant resultant force F accelerates the object from rest: W = Fx = max
M1 · v² = u² + 2ax with u = 0 gives ax = ½v²
A1 · So W = m × ½v² = ½mv², which equals the kinetic energy gained

questions.prompt: A pendulum bob of mass 0.20 kg is pulled aside so that it is 0.15 m above its lowest point, and released from rest. In practice the speed at the lowest point is slightly less than your answer to (a). Explain why.
scheme: B1 · Some energy is transferred to thermal energy (and sound) by work done against air resistance / friction at the pivot

scheme: mgh = 27 470 J; ½mv² = 14 000 J; difference = 1.35 × 10⁴ J.

scheme: B1 · Rate of doing work / work done (energy transferred) per unit time

scheme: C1 · Total mass 1200 kg; P = mgh/t = 1200 × 9.81 × 24 / 16

questions.prompt: A lift (elevator) of mass 900 kg carries four passengers of mass 75 kg each. It rises 24 m at constant speed in 16 s. The electrical input power to the motor is 25 kW. Calculate the efficiency of the system.

B1 · Copper: after the elastic limit a large region of plastic deformation (curve flattens)

questions.prompt: Copper is a ductile material and glass is a brittle material. Define elastic limit.

questions.prompt: What is the ultimate tensile strength?

The stress at which it breaks

levels: Level 3 (5–6)

A clear workable method with all key measurements (L, d, F, x) and the instruments used, a correct graphical analysis giving E = gradient × L/A, and several steps to improve accuracy and safety. Well structured.
Level 2 (3–4)
A workable method with most measurements described and an attempt at analysis that could give E. Some detail missing.
Level 1 (1–2)
A basic method with some relevant measurements or a correct equation, but little detail.
indicative: Long thin wire clamped at one end, over a pulley, with a marker against a fixed metre rule (or Searle's apparatus with vernier)
Measure original length L (≈ 2 m) from clamp to marker with a metre rule / tape
Measure diameter with a micrometer at several points and orientations; average; A = πd²/4
Add masses in equal steps; record extension each time with the marker against the scale; small initial load to straighten the wire
Repeat readings while unloading to check the wire returns to zero (elastic)
Plot force against extension; use the straight-line region
E = gradient × L/A
Safety: goggles, cushion beneath the masses

questions.prompt: A thermometer is placed in a beaker of hot water. Explain what is meant by thermal equilibrium.

B1 · The objects are at the same temperature

questions.prompt: A thermometer is placed in a beaker of hot water. Explain why the thermometer must be left in the water for some time before it is read.
scheme: B1 · So that the thermometer reaches thermal equilibrium with (the same temperature as) the water

questions.prompt: A thermometer is placed in a beaker of hot water. The water is at 65 °C. Convert this temperature to kelvin.
The absolute scale of temperature has its zero at absolute zero. State what is meant by absolute zero.
scheme: B1 · The lowest possible temperature / the temperature at which a substance has minimum internal energy

questions.prompt: The absolute scale of temperature has its zero at absolute zero. The temperature of a gas rises from −40 °C to 60 °C. State the rise in temperature in kelvin.
scheme: B1 · 100 K (a temperature difference is the same in K and °C)

questions.prompt: The absolute scale of temperature has its zero at absolute zero. What is the ratio of the absolute temperature of boiling water (100 °C) to that of melting ice (0 °C)?
Convert normal body temperature, 37 °C, to kelvin.
Liquid nitrogen boils at −196 °C. What is this in kelvin?
The temperature of a room rises by 6 °C. What is the rise in kelvin?
scheme: A kelvin and a degree Celsius are the same size.

questions.prompt: Two objects are in thermal equilibrium. Which statement must be true?
options: They have the same internal energy
They are at the same temperature
They have the same specific heat capacity
No energy moves between them at all
scheme: Equilibrium means no net energy transfer, which happens when the temperatures are equal.

questions.prompt: What happens at absolute zero?
options: All particles stop moving and internal energy is zero
The particles have their minimum possible kinetic energy
scheme: Absolute zero is the temperature at which a substance has minimum internal energy.

t2.title: The kinetic model of matter and Brownian motion

questions.prompt: Brownian motion can be observed using smoke particles in air. Describe how Brownian motion can be observed.
scheme: B1 · Smoke is trapped in a small (sealed) glass cell
B1 · The cell is illuminated (brightly) from the side
B1 · It is viewed through a microscope; the smoke particles are seen as bright specks

questions.prompt: Brownian motion can be observed using smoke particles in air. Describe the motion of the smoke particles.
Brownian motion can be observed using smoke particles in air. Explain what this motion shows about the air molecules.
scheme: B1 · Air molecules are moving rapidly and randomly
B1 · They are much smaller than the smoke particles, and unequal numbers of collisions on different sides give a random resultant force

questions.prompt: The kinetic model describes solids, liquids and gases in terms of their particles. Describe the arrangement and motion of the particles in a liquid, and compare them with those in a gas.
scheme: B1 · Liquid: particles close together (similar spacing to a solid), with no regular arrangement
B1 · Liquid: particles move randomly and slide past each other
B1 · Gas: particles far apart, moving rapidly and randomly with negligible forces between them

questions.prompt: The kinetic model describes solids, liquids and gases in terms of their particles. At 100 °C, liquid water has a density of 960 kg m⁻³ and water vapour has a density of 0.60 kg m⁻³. Estimate the ratio of the mean separation of molecules in the vapour to that in the liquid.
scheme: C1 · Ratio of volume per molecule = 960 / 0.60 = 1600

questions.prompt: In which state of matter do the particles vibrate about fixed positions?
scheme: In a solid, the particles are held in a fixed lattice and vibrate about their positions.

questions.prompt: Smoke particles in air are seen to move randomly. What causes this movement?
options: Uneven bombardment by fast-moving air molecules
The light used to illuminate them
scheme: At any instant more molecules hit one side than the other, giving a random resultant force.

questions.prompt: Steam is about 1000 times less dense than water. Roughly how many times further apart are the molecules in steam?
scheme: Volume per molecule is 1000 times larger, so the spacing is ∛1000 = 10 times larger.

questions.prompt: The temperature of the air in a smoke cell is increased. What happens to the motion of the smoke particles?
scheme: The air molecules move faster, so the collisions are harder and the smoke particles move more vigorously.

questions.prompt: Why are the air molecules themselves not seen under the microscope?
options: They only exist in the dark
scheme: Molecules are far smaller than the wavelength of light and the resolution of a light microscope.

t3.title: Internal energy and changes of state

questions.prompt: A solid is heated at a constant rate. Its temperature rises, stays constant at 80 °C for some time, then rises again. Define internal energy.
scheme: B1 · The sum of the kinetic and potential energies of the particles (atoms or molecules)

questions.prompt: A solid is heated at a constant rate. Its temperature rises, stays constant at 80 °C for some time, then rises again. Explain, in terms of the particles, why the temperature stays constant at 80 °C.
scheme: B1 · The substance is melting (changing state)
B1 · The energy supplied breaks bonds / increases the separation of the particles, increasing their potential energy
B1 · The mean kinetic energy of the particles does not change, so the temperature stays constant

questions.prompt: A solid is heated at a constant rate. Its temperature rises, stays constant at 80 °C for some time, then rises again. The temperature rises at a different rate after the constant section. Suggest why.
scheme: B1 · The liquid has a different specific heat capacity from the solid

questions.prompt: Water boils at 100 °C. Explain why the internal energy of 1 kg of steam at 100 °C is greater than that of 1 kg of water at 100 °C.
scheme: B1 · The temperature is the same, so the mean kinetic energy of the molecules is the same
B1 · The molecules in steam are much further apart, so they have more potential energy

questions.prompt: Water boils at 100 °C. A gas is cooled at constant volume without changing state. What happens to its internal energy?
options: It decreases, because the kinetic energy of the molecules decreases
It decreases, because the potential energy of the molecules decreases

options: The total kinetic energy of the particles
The sum of the randomly distributed kinetic and potential energies of the particles
The energy stored in the bonds of the particles
The temperature multiplied by the mass
scheme: Internal energy includes both the random kinetic energy and the potential energy of the particles.

questions.prompt: While ice melts at 0 °C, what happens to the particles?
options: Kinetic energy increases, potential energy constant
Kinetic energy constant, potential energy increases
scheme: The temperature is constant, so the mean kinetic energy is constant; energy goes into breaking bonds.

questions.prompt: How long does a 2.0 kW heater take to melt 0.50 kg of ice at 0 °C? (L = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹)
Water vapour condenses on a cold window. What happens to its internal energy?
scheme: Bonds form and the potential energy of the molecules decreases; energy is released to the window.

questions.prompt: Why does boiling need more energy per kilogram than melting?

scheme: Boiling breaks all the remaining bonds and the vapour expands against the atmosphere.

questions.prompt: A student determines the specific heat capacity of a 1.00 kg aluminium block. The heater has a p.d. of 12.0 V and a current of 3.2 A. In 8.0 minutes the temperature of the block rises from 18.5 °C to 37.0 °C. Define specific heat capacity.

A clear and complete description of the formation and of both life cycles, with correct final states and the reasons for them (degeneracy pressure, Chandrasekhar limit, core collapse). Correct movement on the HR diagram for both stars. The answer is well structured and uses correct terms.

A clear method that would work, including measuring background, recording counts in regular short intervals as the activity falls, and correcting for background. md8.title: Doppler imaging: measuring the speed of blood

questions.prompt: Doppler ultrasound is used to measure the speed of blood in an artery. Explain why the frequency of the ultrasound reflected from the blood differs from the emitted frequency.
scheme: B1 · The red blood cells are moving relative to the transducer
B1 · Doppler effect: the frequency increases if they move towards the probe (decreases if away); the shift occurs on reception and re-emission

questions.prompt: Doppler ultrasound is used to measure the speed of blood in an artery. 8.0 MHz ultrasound is directed at 30° to blood flowing at 0.25 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency shift.
Doppler ultrasound is used to measure the speed of blood in an artery. Explain why the probe must not be held perpendicular to the artery.
scheme: B1 · cos 90° = 0, so there would be no frequency shift

questions.prompt: A frequency shift of 3.2 kHz is measured using 5.0 MHz ultrasound at 45° to the flow. Calculate the speed of the blood.

scheme: B1 · Blood flows faster through the narrowing (same volume per second through a smaller area), so the shift is larger

questions.prompt: 5.0 MHz ultrasound is reflected by blood moving at 0.30 m s⁻¹ directly towards the probe (θ = 0). What is the frequency shift? (c = 1540 m s⁻¹)
The same blood flow is measured with the beam at 60° to the vessel. What is the shift now?
scheme: cos 60° = 0.5, so the shift halves: 974 Hz.

questions.prompt: Why is there a factor of 2 in the Doppler equation for ultrasound?
options: The shift occurs twice: the cells receive a shifted frequency and then re-emit it as moving sources
The wave travels at twice the speed
scheme: The moving cell acts as a moving observer and then a moving source.

indicative: X-ray: attenuation (photoelectric, Compton); shadow image; good for bone; contrast media for soft organs; small ionising dose
CAT: rotating X-ray tube and detectors; computer reconstruction of slices; 3D, distinguishes soft tissues; larger dose; expensive
PET: β⁺ tracer (F-18 FDG); annihilation photons detected in coincidence; shows function / metabolic activity; dose from tracer; cyclotron needed; expensive

questions.prompt: A student wants to test whether the period T of a mass–spring oscillator is related to the mass m by T = 2π√(m/k), and to determine the spring constant k. Describe how the student could carry out the experiment and analyse the results to test the relationship and determine k.
levels: Level 3 (5–6)

A clear, workable method: how m is varied and how T is measured, with steps for accuracy. A correct graph of T² against m (or T against √m) with what a straight line through the origin shows, and k correctly obtained from the gradient. Well structured and logical.
Level 2 (3–4)

A workable method for measuring T for different masses with some accuracy steps. An attempt at a graph or analysis which could lead to k, though some detail or the link to the relationship is missing.
Level 1 (1–2)
A basic method that measures T for at least one mass, or a simple statement of analysis. Limited detail and structure.
indicative: Hang the spring from a clamp stand; add slotted masses to a hanger and record the total mass (including hanger) on a balance
Displace the mass a small distance vertically and release it; use a fiducial marker at the equilibrium position
Time 10 (or 20) oscillations with a stopwatch and divide; repeat and average
Alternatively use a motion sensor / data logger
Repeat for at least 5–6 different masses over a wide range
Check the spring is not stretched beyond its elastic limit
Plot T² against m: a straight line through the origin confirms T² ∝ m
Gradient = 4π²/k, so k = 4π²/gradient

Clear description of both pieces of evidence (galactic redshift with Hubble's law and the CMB), each explained correctly as evidence for an expanding universe that was once hot and dense. Well structured, with correct use of terms such as redshift, recession and wavelength stretching.

A clear, correctly ordered account of the formation and evolution of a low-mass star (nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, planetary nebula, white dwarf) with explanation of the key processes (gravitational collapse, fusion, equilibrium between radiation pressure and gravity, electron degeneracy pressure), and a correct comparison with a massive star (red supergiant, supernova, neutron star or black hole).

questions.prompt: Light and electrons both show wave and particle behaviour. Explain how the photoelectric effect provides evidence for the particle nature of light, and how electron diffraction provides evidence for the wave nature of matter. Discuss what is meant by wave–particle duality.
levels: Level 3 (5–6)

A clear explanation of the photoelectric observations (threshold frequency, instantaneous emission, KE independent of intensity) and how only the photon model explains them; a clear description of electron diffraction and the de Broglie relation; and a coherent statement of wave–particle duality.
Level 2 (3–4)
Correct key evidence for both, with some explanation, or one explained in full.
Level 1 (1–2)
Some relevant statements with little explanation.
indicative: Electrons are emitted only if the frequency is above a threshold, whatever the intensity
KEmax depends on frequency, not intensity; emission is instantaneous
Wave model predicts any frequency would work given enough time / intensity: it fails
Photon model: energy hf in discrete packets, one photon to one electron, hf = φ + KEmax
Electrons through thin graphite produce diffraction rings on a screen; diffraction is a wave property
λ = h/p; higher accelerating p.d. gives smaller rings
Duality: light and matter show wave behaviour (propagation, diffraction) and particle behaviour (emission, absorption, detection)
